about: Part of the reference catalogue: the case studies, designs and worked examples of chapters 1 and 2 of Goos and Jones,
Optimal Design of Experiments: A Case Study Approach (2011), for testing that software reproduces them. source: the
citation, with what was read and when. experiments: the extraction experiment, with its factors, response and runs as
printed, where it is printed, and expected: every number the book prints for it, as printed text, with where it is
printed (a page and a quotation) and check: how to recompute it, or manual, the reason it is not recomputed. A check
with a disagreement records a number known not to reproduce and why. The book fits every model in coded units, and
its VIF is n times a coefficient's variance in units of sigma squared (Equation 2.13): the library's coefficient
variance from evaluate_design's information_matrix, times the run count. An alias matrix printed in thirds is
compared entry by entry as arithmetic (expression). designs: the splits of chapter 1's runs between two machines or
two treatments (allocate_runs: each split's variance, its root and its efficiency), Table 2.4's bias calculation
(product_column, the mean of a product column), the four-run design of Table 2.8, the D-optimal design of Table
2.11, and the designs of the coordinate-exchange example, each compared on |X'X| (information_matrix, determinant).
not_captured: what in these pages is not an experiment with data. Read with
every number that has a check.

source.title: Optimal Design of Experiments: A Case Study Approach
source.cite: Goos, P. and Jones, B. (2011), Optimal Design of Experiments: A Case Study Approach, Wiley
source.read: 2026-10-18, from a PDF of chapters 1 and 2 (pp. 1 to 45, one PDF page a book page), supplied by the user; every number copied from the PDF's text layer and checked against the page, and Table 2.7, whose text layer drops a row of zeros, read from the page image at 220 dpi

design.type: 12-run two-level orthogonal design, one that can be derived from a Plackett-Burman design
design.details: made by a computer algorithm for a D-optimal design for the main-effects model; six factors, 12 runs, no replicates and no centre runs

runs.notes: Table 2.3 in its printed order; its settings are those of Table 2.2, and Table 2.1 prints the same runs coded −1 and +1 (a solvent absent and present, pH and time at their low and high levels)

experiments.notes: The book fits every model in coded units, x = (setting − centre)/(half the range), the factors x1 to x6 in the order of the columns. GeneBe's current process, methanol at neutral pH for 2 hours, yields about 25 mg; management wants more than 45 mg; at most 15 runs could be afforded, of which 12 are run and three kept for a confirmatory experiment. Dr. Zheng's model (Equation 2.1) keeps the main effects significant at the 5% level in the main-effects model, and the design being orthogonal, their coefficients are the same as in that model. The book's VIF is n times a coefficient's relative variance, its variance in units of σ² (Equation 2.13), checked as the library's coefficient variance times the run count.

2.1 (pp. 9 and 10): the key concepts, no data

2.2.1 (pp. 10 to 14): GeneBe's process in words: cultures grown at 37 °C for 24 hours and then at 30 °C to 33 °C, 100 ml of culture per extraction, the current yield of about 25 mg, the target of more than 45 mg, and a budget of at most 15 runs, of which 12 are used and three kept for a confirmatory experiment; context, held in the extraction entry's notes
2.2.2 (p. 15): the all-subsets regression of all models with up to seven effects, which finds the ethanol-by-propanol interaction; the models it compares are not printed

2.3.1 to 2.3.4 (pp. 21 to 26): the main-effects and two-factor interaction models (Equations 2.3 to 2.5, Attachments 2.1 and 2.2), factor scaling (Equation 2.6), least squares (Equations 2.7 to 2.11), and the conditions under which X'X is diagonal with n on its diagonal, so that each relative variance takes its minimum, 1/n: formulas, no data
2.3.5 (pp. 27 and 28): significance tests and power in words, with Fisher's (1926) cutoff of 5% and the false positive rate of one test in 10,000 at a cutoff of 0.0001; no power is computed

2.3.6 (pp. 28 and 29): the variance inflation factor (Equation 2.13), the rule of thumb that a VIF above five signals collinearity, and that a VIF of four doubles a confidence interval: definitions, applied in Tables 2.10 and 2.12
2.3.7 (pp. 29 to 31): the alias matrix A = (X1'X1)^-1 X1'X2 (Equations 2.14 to 2.18), derived; applied in Tables 2.7 and 2.9

2.3.8 (pp. 33 and 34): D-optimality, the determinant (1/n)^p of (X'X)^-1 for an orthogonal design, and that no orthogonal two-level design exists when the run count is not a multiple of 4: statements, no data
2.3.9.1 and 2.3.9.2 (pp. 35 to 37): the coordinate-exchange algorithm in words, with the advice to use at least 1000 random starts
Figure 2.3 (p. 38): the designs of the worked example plotted, held as goos-jones-coordinate-exchange-two-factors
2.3.10 (p. 41): the statement that no 12-run two-level design has orthogonal columns for the six main effects and the one interaction; no number

2.3.11 (pp. 41 to 43): sparsity, hierarchy and heredity, the 80-20 rule, and Li et al. (2006)'s reanalysis of 113 published full factorial experiments with three to seven factors, which found 80% of the active two-factor interactions synergistic: the findings of another source, without its data
2.4 and 2.5 (pp. 44 and 45): background reading and the summary, no data
